newsitem.title: NORWAY: France's GdF sees Euro gas bubble bursting by 2010.
newsitem.headline: France's GdF sees Euro gas bubble bursting by 2010.

text.p: The European gas market will face a supply shortfall early next decade and will require major investment if supplies are to remain in step with burgeoning demand, Gaz de France (GdF) said on Tuesday.

Claude Detourne, director of production and transmission at the French state gas monopoly, said demand for gas was forecast to increase sharply early next century with more than 130 billion cubic metres (bcm) of additional consumption by 2010.

"The current market situation, with the British gas bubble and the revised estimation of North Sea gas production capacities, masks the gas industry's true structural situation and may give rise to a mistaken belief that structural overcapacity is a long term reality," Detourne told the 5th International Gas Transport Symposium in Bergen on the west coast of Norway.
"In fact, the experience of gas companies such as GdF shows clearly...that the current bubble will not be sufficient to satisfy demand increases up to the year 2010 and beyond."
Detourne said there was a risk of the European gas bubble bursting between 2005 and 2010 depending on growth in the electricity sector.

The deficit would leave the industry facing two major challenges, he said. The need to mobilise distant gas reserves while remaining competitive with other energy sources and to closer gas supplies, and the guarantee of security of supplies under the best conditions and lowest costs in a context where 50 percent of supplies come from outside the European Union and Norway.

New resources will be found in remote areas of the North Sea and Barents Sea, Russia -- the Yamal peninsula in particular, the southern Sahara in Algeria, the Middle East, the Gulf of Guinea and from Central and Latin America.

These will call for the development of new transmission infrastructures several thousands of kilometres in length, for the implementation of new liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals and the construction of new ships, and for the extension of national transmission systems and storage facilities in Europe, Detourne said.

"To meet these challenges, major capital investment will be indispensable. For example, the investment necessary to implement an LNG supply chain to deliver 25 bcm per year of gas from the Middle East to Europe can be estimated around $15 billion, not counting production field development costs," he said.

Technological progress would also be essential to reduce costs. Improved technology would make it possible to build LNG carriers with a capacity of 200,000 cubic metres, or to increase the size of liquefaction plants, or in the offshore sector, to lay deeper pipelines and to develop new offshore gas fields at depths of 500 to 1,000 metres, such as those located around the Shetland Islands.
He added that institutional regulations governing the European gas market should be defined as soon as possible with operating rules established to take into account long-term concerns.

"Major investments will have to be made by all players along the gas supply chain to enable the industry to satisfy accelerating demand over the coming years and we believe that these efforts will be possible and will bear fruit only if the industry is able to plan its future reliably over the long term," Detourne said.
